title: Guidelines for Early Food Introduction and Patterns of Food Allergy
source: Show notes list only the DOI; no abstract text or figures were provided with the episode.
one_line: A Pediatrics study examining how changes in infant feeding guidelines toward early allergenic food introduction relate to observed patterns of food allergy in children.
key_claims: The episode's source material provides only the DOI, so no specific effect sizes, prevalence figures, or confidence intervals from the paper can be recorded here.
Central framing: guideline shifts away from delayed allergen introduction toward early introduction are the exposure of interest, with childhood food allergy patterns as the outcome.
limitations: No numerical results, cohort size, or statistical methods were available in the supplied material, so the strength of the reported association cannot be assessed from this card.

Population-level guideline-change studies of this design generally cannot establish that guideline adoption caused changes in allergy rates, since secular trends and diagnostic practice shifts co-occur.
Authors' own stated limitations were not included in the material provided.
open_questions: What were the actual measured allergy rates before and after the guideline change, and over what time window?
Was individual-level adherence to early introduction measured, or only guideline era as a proxy?
Would a randomised or quasi-experimental design separate guideline effects from changing diagnostic and ascertainment practices?
Do the patterns differ by specific allergen (peanut, egg, milk) and by baseline infant risk category?
